ABSTRACT

TRADITIONAL ECOLOGICAL KNOWLEDGE IN GLEANING FISHERIES AS POTENTIAL INPUTS FOR CULTURALLY RELEVANT SCIENCE CURRICULUM

Journal: Environment & Ecosystem Science (EES)

Author:Michael G. Garlan

This is an open access article distributed under the Creative Commons Attribution License CC BY 4.0, which permits unrestricted use, distribution, and reproduction in any medium, provided the original work is properly cited

DOI: 10.26480/ees.01.2026.65.70

Gleaning fisheries represent a valuable yet underutilized resource for contextualizing science teaching in coastal communities. Grounded on the traditional ecological knowledge (TEK) framework, this study utilized ethnographic methods to document the indigenous knowledge embedded in gleaning fisheries and map its potential contribution to contextualized science curriculum. Data were collected through participant observation, semi-structured interviews with experienced gleaners, and field documentation of ecological practices and analyzed using Spradley’s analytic framework. The findings reveal that gleaners possess inherent ecological knowledge related to species classification, reproductive cycles, tidal patterns, habitat characteristics, and sustainable harvesting strategies. These knowledge domains correspond with scientific concepts in biology, ecology, earth science, and environmental science. The study demonstrates how community-based ecological knowledge can serve as contextual inputs for science curriculum development and culturally relevant pedagogy. By bridging traditional ecological knowledge with formal science education, the study contributes to ongoing global discussions on integrating indigenous knowledge systems into science curricula and highlights the potential of coastal livelihood practices as pedagogical resources for contextualized science teaching.
